summary: A protocol analysis report on extensions to RIP for demand circuits, documenting key features and implementation experience, as required by the Routing Protocol Criteria.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC analyzes extensions that let RIP operate over on-demand circuits without sending periodic updates across a quiet link. It describes the mechanisms, restrictions, and implementation experience reported at the time.

questions: how does demand rip reduce costs
subtitle: An analysis of RIP extensions for networks that establish circuits on demand.

tldr.problem: Periodic routing updates can be costly on wide-area networks where circuits are switched on demand.
tldr.mechanism: Demand RIP sends triggered updates, uses a circuit manager to establish connections when needed, and assumes received routes remain valid until the path is known to be down.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1581 documents the proposal and implementation experience. It requires predictable detection of unreachability and bidirectional calling ability.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1581 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo is an analysis of the Demand RIP extension described in RFC 1582.

sections.title: Why Use Demand RIP
sections.content:
RFC 1581 reports on extensions to RIP for wide-area networks. Demand RIP is intended for links where regular routing or service updates would be too costly in money or packet overhead, including switched X.25 or ISDN networks and some point-to-point links.

It requires an underlying mechanism that can determine unreachability within a finite, predictable period. On LANs, an implementation can run standard RIP and interoperate with implementations following the original specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Demand RIP targets links where frequent check-in messages are undesirable. It still needs a reliable way to learn when a path has actually failed.

sections.title: Triggered Updates and Circuit Management
sections.content:
On wide-area networks, updates are sent when a routing-database event occurs rather than through periodic broadcasts. Each update is retransmitted until acknowledged, and received information does not time out while the path is presumed reachable. The response format adds sequence and fragment information, and the extension defines an acknowledgement packet.

A circuit manager establishes a connection to the next-hop router when data or an update needs to be sent and closes it after inactivity. If connection attempts fail, it reports the circuit down and retries at increasing intervals. Once connected, it reports the circuit up.
sections.plainLanguage: The router opens a circuit when it has information to send. It sends updates only when routes change, and retries an update until it receives an acknowledgment.

sections.title: Reachability, Limits, and Security
sections.content:
On a stable network, the most recently received route information is assumed accurate even when no circuit is currently open. If the circuit manager determines that the path is not operational, the stored information is timed out. When a circuit returns, the peers exchange full routing information.

The RFC reports one completed implementation at the time, tested on X.25 and ISDN and with RIP implementations on Ethernet LANs. Demand RIP requires calls to be possible in both directions and cannot support third-party route advertisement on the WAN. Incoming updates are checked using both physical and logical addresses; RIP-2 authentication can add protection where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: A quiet circuit does not mean its routes are lost; they remain trusted until the path is declared down. Both ends must be able to call, and updates must come from an accepted address.
